extracted.intended_audience: federal courts, patent litigators, in-house counsel, and patent holders
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standard and equitable framework governing whether a district court should grant a permanent injunction in a patent-infringement suit, as articulated by the U.S. Supreme Court in eBay Inc. v. MercExchange. Focuses on application of traditional equity principles to Patent Act disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional four-factor test for permanent injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff seeking a permanent injunction must satisfy a four-factor test historically employed by courts of equity: (1) that it has suffered an irreparable injury; (2) that remedies available at law are inadequate to compensate for that injury; (3) that, considering the balance of hardships between the plaintiff and defendant, a remedy in equity is warranted; and (4) that the public interest would not be disserved by a permanent injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is derived from equity practice (see Weinberger v. Romero-Barcelo and Amoco Production Co.) and applies to disputes under the Patent Act; the decision to grant or deny relief is an act of equitable discretion by the district court and is reviewable on appeal for abuse of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreparable injury
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must demonstrate that it has suffered an irreparable injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A court should not adopt categorical rules that certain facts (e.g., a plaintiff’s willingness to license or lack of commercial activity) automatically establish no irreparable harm. Some patent holders (e.g., university researchers or independent inventors) may reasonably license rather than practice patents yet still suffer irreparable injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies at law are inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must show that remedies available at law, such as monetary damages, are inadequate to compensate for the injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where monetary compensation cannot make the plaintiff whole (for example, harm to exclusionary rights or where the patent is central to business), injunctive relief may be appropriate; conversely, when the patented invention is a small component of a product, legal damages may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of hardships favors equitable relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Considering the balance of hardships between plaintiff and defendant, a remedy in equity is warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must weigh the relative hardships and may deny an injunction if enjoining the defendant would impose undue hardship relative to the plaintiff’s injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting a permanent injunction must not disserve the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-interest implications (including competition, access to important technologies, and broader economic effects) are a discrete factor and may counsel against an injunction even if other factors favor the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable discretion and appellate review
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision to grant or deny permanent injunctive relief is an act of equitable discretion by the district court, reviewable on appeal for abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 283 of the Patent Act provides that injunctions may issue 'in accordance with the principles of equity.' Courts should exercise 'considerable discretion' consistent with established legal standards and history, and appellate courts should defer unless there is an abuse of that discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: No categorical entitlement to injunction upon finding validity and infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A general rule that a permanent injunction will issue once infringement and validity have been adjudged is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit’s ‘general rule’ that injunctions issue automatically absent exceptional circumstances was rejected; courts must apply the four-factor equitable test rather than apply a per se rule in favor of injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on categorical denials based on licensing or non-practicing status
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorical rules denying injunctions because a patentee is willing to license or is not commercially practicing the patent are impermissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such categorical denials conflict with traditional equity principles and precedent (e.g., Continental Paper Bag Co.). Courts should evaluate the actual harm and circumstances rather than presumptively denying relief based on licensing behavior or nonuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory right to exclude does not dictate remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act’s grant that patents have the 'right to exclude' does not automatically entitle a patentee to an injunction; creation of a right is distinct from the remedies for its violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 261 (attributes of personal property) must be read subject to the remedial provisions of the Patent Act (including §283), which ties injunctive relief to equity principles rather than to an automatic remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of modern patent practices and patent type
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should account for the changing nature of patent holders and patents—e.g., entities that primarily license patents and business-method patents—when applying the equitable factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In situations where patentees use injunctions as bargaining leverage or where patents are vague/suspect (e.g., certain business-method patents), the four-factor calculus (particularly adequacy of legal remedies and public interest) may weigh against injunctions. History is instructive but courts must determine whether past practice fits current circumstances.
